notes.read: A shaggy Highland cow standing in tall grass at sunset, lit from behind on the right. What matters is the cow's face, horns and the gold rim of light on its coat; the hard parts are the hair and the grass, which the beginner version turned into repeated locks and flicks. The lesson is about painting far things fast, then building an animal light over dark.
notes.order: Back to front, as the paint-along goes: sky, far hills and loch, hillside and meadow cover the canvas first. Then the cow is built as a teacher draws it: a flat shape, its shadow, horns, locks dark to light, then the face. The tall grass goes over its legs after that, and the gold rim and brightest lights go on last, over everything.

steps.blend-sky: Everything sits on the sky, so it goes first and runs past the hill line.
steps.lay-clouds: The cloud streaks go on the dry sky, before the hills cover their lower part.
steps.light-clouds: The lit tops go over the streaks once they're dry, finishing the sky.
steps.lay-hills: The far hills overlap the sky, so they come right after it, painted down past the hillside line.
steps.shade-hills: Shading the near range separates the two ranges while the violet is still the top layer.
steps.lay-loch: The loch sits at the foot of the hills, before the hillside meets it.
steps.lay-hillside: The olive hillside goes over the violet base, below the hills and loch.
steps.patch-hillside: Dark patches on the dry olive make the hillside roll back.
steps.lay-meadow: The meadow is the nearest ground, under where the cow and grass go.
steps.block-cow: The cow goes on the finished background as one flat shape, the base for everything on it.
steps.shade-cow: Its shadow side goes on next, dark under light, before any hair.
steps.block-horns: The horns rise from the head, so the head has to be there first.
steps.shade-horns: The horns' shading goes on the dry cream, before the locks cover their bases.
steps.locks-ginger: The main locks go over the shaded shape, dark coat left showing between them.
steps.locks-tan: Lighter locks go over the ginger ones: light over dark.
steps.paint-nose: The nose goes under the finished fringe so the fringe hangs over it.
steps.nostrils-mouth: The dark dots go on the dry nose and finish the face.
steps.flick-dark-grass: The tall grass comes after the cow so it grows over its legs; the dark blades first.
steps.flick-light-grass: Sunlit blades go over the dark ones, light over dark.
steps.flick-seed-heads: Gold seed heads sit on the tips of the finished blades.
steps.rim-cow: The rim light goes over the finished coat, near the end, so nothing covers it.
steps.last-lights: The brightest touches go on last, on the horns and the grass tips.

stages.name: Blend the sunset sky
steps: Start with Sky blue at the top edge of the canvas, stroking side to side across the full width.
Work down in long side-to-side strokes. Without rinsing, pick up Warm gold and paint it in, then stroke back up over the join several times while both are wet.
The blue band is about 5 1/4 in tall, starting at the top edge. Warm gold fills everything from there to the bottom edge, since hills and land go over it later.
Leave no white canvas anywhere. A few soft, deeper orange streaks in the gold can stay; you don't need to smooth them all away.
The whole canvas is covered: clear blue at the top edge melting into warm gold with no hard line. If a line shows, add more gold at the join and blend again.

Keep the strokes broken so blue sky shows through and between them. Leave the lower sky alone.
Ragged, flat gold streaks cross the blue, thickest toward the right edge, with sky peeking through. If one went on solid, let it dry before going on.

Violet covers the canvas from the peaks to the bottom edge, paler along the far ridge, with soft wavy ridge lines. No shading yet.

opening.welcome: You're about to paint a shaggy Highland cow standing in tall summer grass at sunset, with violet hills and a gold sky behind it. The heart of it is the cow's face: the glowing fringe, the soft nose and the two curved horns.
opening.light: The light is the low sun, sitting behind the cow near the hills. It makes the sky glow gold, leaves most of the cow's coat in shade, and catches a bright gold rim along the fringe, the sunlit side of the cow and the grass tips.

skills.how: Press the full width of the angle brush, then turn onto its edge and lighten as you pull, so each mark tapers to a point. It builds the cow's whole shaggy coat, lock by lock, and its gold rim. Leave gaps so the darker coat shows between the locks.

A quick stroke up from the base of a blade, lifting off so the tip thins. It makes the tall grass and lets it grow over the cow's legs. Keep the brush lightly loaded, since too much paint makes flat blobs, and let each lighter pass thin out as it goes.

Only the tip of a dry brush goes in the paint, skimmed lightly so the marks break up and catch the canvas texture. It lays the cloud streaks, the soft hill shadows and the last bright lights. If it goes on solid, the brush was too loaded.

opening.road: First you blend the sky and dry-brush its clouds, because everything else sits on it. Next come the far hills and the sliver of loch, then the rolling hillside and the meadow, so the whole canvas is covered before the cow arrives. The cow is built the way a teacher draws it: a flat shape, its shadow, then the horns. Then its coat goes on lock by lock, light over dark, and the face comes after that. The tall grass is flicked on next so it grows over the cow's legs, and the gold rim and brightest lights go on last.

the-sky.for: This stage covers the canvas with a smooth sunset sky and its gold cloud streaks.
the-sky.end: The canvas is all sky now, clear blue melting into warm gold, with ragged lit cloud streaks.

the-hills-and-loch.for: This stage lays in the distant violet hills, shades the nearer range, and adds the pale sliver of loch.
the-hills-and-loch.end: Two ranges of violet hills sit against the sunset, the nearer one darker, with a thin silver strip of loch tucked against them.

the-land.for: This stage builds the rolling green hillside and the meadow, so the whole canvas is covered before the cow.
the-land.end: Striped green hillside rolls back toward the hills, and a textured green-and-gold meadow fills the front of the canvas.

the-cow-shape.for: This stage builds the cow as a flat shape, gives it a shadow side, and adds its two horns.
the-cow-shape.end: A rounded, dark-streaked brown cow stands in the meadow with two gray-brown curved horns, still with no locks or face.

the-shaggy-coat.for: This stage pulls the cow's long locks of hair, light over dark, so the coat looks shaggy.
the-shaggy-coat.end: The cow is covered in long hanging ginger and honey locks, its eyes hidden by the fringe.

the-face.for: This stage gives the cow its face: the rounded nose, the nostrils and the mouth.
the-face.end: A soft dusty-pink nose with dark nostrils and a mouth line peeks out from the fringe.

the-tall-grass.for: This stage flicks the tall grass over the meadow and the cow's legs, dark blades first, then sunlit ones and seed heads.
the-tall-grass.end: Tall grass with dark and sunlit blades and gold seed heads rises around the cow and hides its legs.

the-last-lights.for: This stage adds the low sun's last touches: the gold rim on the cow and the brightest lights.
the-last-lights.end: The painting is finished: the cow glows along its fringe and sunlit side, the horns catch the light, and the grass tips shine.

technique_picks.technique_why: A sunset landscape with one big animal in front is the classic back-to-front paint-along: blend the sky, lay the hills and land over it, then build the cow in long strokes and flick the grass over its legs.
